summary:
Visitors stand under the United States federal framework in every state. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, and new passport applications are issued only as M or F from the supporting documents submitted, while passports already bearing an X remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant declaring a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.

Facility use is regulated across a substantial part of the country. Bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans by gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement has occurred: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Kansas sits at the restrictive end of that pattern. SB 244, signed in February 2026, confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in government buildings and creates new civil and criminal penalties, including a private right of action under which an individual may sue a person suspected of a violation for roughly $1,000. The law bars updating driver's licences and state IDs and invalidates existing licences whose gender marker is inconsistent with sex assigned at birth. The Department of Revenue has been mailing written notice, and many holders have already been told their licence is now invalid.

Kansas is one of four states designated do-not-travel for trans people. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the most recent addition, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends. An earlier assessment dated 20 February 2026 moved Kansas from 'Worst Laws' to 'Do Not Travel', the first such addition in a year, following the bathroom-bounty provision that lets private individuals sue trans people encountered in wrong-sex facilities.

Litigation is already running. Within days of SB 244's enactment in late February 2026, two trans men filed Doe v. State of Kansas in Douglas County District Court, represented by the ACLU and Ballard Spahr, citing fear of violence under the bathroom-restriction and ID-invalidation law.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country, advisories that followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.
tangentialFactors:
The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions, so the rules encountered depend heavily on the state involved. Kansas's position on that map is among the most restrictive, but neighbouring and other states differ, and a visitor's exposure to document checks varies accordingly.

The federal document and entry rules apply irrespective of state law, so a trans visitor to Kansas faces both layers at once: national passport and visa treatment, screening procedures at federal checkpoints, and a state regime covering facilities and state-issued identification.

The do-not-travel designations are drawn from recurring national legal risk assessments rather than from any government advisory, and their count has moved over the course of 2026; Kansas was flagged in February 2026 and Idaho in July 2026.
localsOnly:
Kansas residents may no longer change the gender marker on a driver's licence or state ID, and licences already carrying a corrected marker have been invalidated under SB 244. The Department of Revenue has mailed written notice to holders, and many have been told directly that their licence is no longer valid.

Residents are confined to birth-sex facilities in government buildings under the statute, with violations carrying new civil and criminal penalties. The civil provision permits private individuals to sue a person they suspect of a violation for approximately $1,000, an exposure that applies to people encountered in facilities rather than to officials acting alone.

Two Kansas residents have already sued: Doe v. State of Kansas was filed in Douglas County District Court in late February 2026 by two trans men represented by the ACLU and Ballard Spahr, challenging both the bathroom restriction and the licence invalidation on the ground that the law exposes them to violence.

Change of marker on birth certificates is barred on the same terms, and rights groups describe the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following, with further targeting bills pending in the state.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any provision of SB 244 has been enjoined or narrowed by court order since enactment is not resolved in the available sources; the February 2026 lawsuit is documented as filed, but no ruling is sourced here.

The precise scope of the facility restriction, which government buildings it reaches, and the operative definition of a violation are described in general terms by the ACLU of Kansas FAQ but the statutory text itself is not in the inventory.

Whether the licence invalidation affects a visitor holding an out-of-state licence, or only Kansas-issued documents, is not stated in the sources and remains unresolved.

The exact number of states currently designated do-not-travel varies by assessment date; two assessments are cited, dated 20 February 2026 and 13 July 2026, and the four-state total is taken from the later one.

Hate-crime protection, healthcare access, partner and marriage recognition, and school-specific rules for visitors are not covered by the available sources for Kansas and are therefore unsourced here.
